paras: The lynching of an unidentified man near Eastman, Georgia, took place on July 14, 1903, when a mob of about fifty men hanged and shot a Black man in southern Dodge County, believing him to be Ed Claus, accused of assaulting a white woman near Darien Junction. Late-July wires from Atlanta and Savannah reported that the dead man was innocent and that Claus had been found alive, and papers North and South and in the Black press then treated it as a mob killing the wrong man.

According to the Brunswick Daily News, Minnie Johnson, a young white woman living near Darien Junction, was beaten "into insensibility" and assaulted by a Black man on Thursday morning, July 9. The accused was named as Ed Claus, a railroad worker whom one dispatch called "well known" locally and another a stranger lately come from "Glenn county"; the county commissioners offered a $200 reward.

On July 10 a railroad agent at Everett City held a stranger who gave his name as Louis Olsen, but the man escaped and shots fired after him missed. Another Black man answering the description was arrested but, a Brunswick dispatch said, "proved to be the wrong man before the mob got at him." Early on July 11 Sheriff Overstreet of Wayne County found a man taken to be Claus on a railroad trestle south of Jesup and shot him twice with buckshot; he escaped wounded into a swamp.

An Eastman dispatch dated July 14 reported that a mob of fifty men, having followed the fugitive through seven counties, found him asleep in a swamp that morning. By this account he declared his innocence and begged for his life, but Miss Johnson "stated positively that he was the criminal." He was hanged from a tree limb, the mob fired pistols and rifles into the body, and the body was left hanging. That afternoon four white men with Winchesters and bloodhounds passed through Savannah toward McIntosh County, saying they had been "out killing a nigger."

The Brunswick Daily News doubted the reports, believing Claus was hidden near Brentwood. On July 26 dispatches said the mob, described as Liberty County men or citizens of Liberty and McIntosh counties, had killed the wrong man, and that Claus had been found in a village near Darien Junction. The Wichita Searchlight added that Governor Terrell had offered a $300 reward for Claus. No report found names the dead man or describes an inquest, arrests of the mob, or a trial of Claus; the Seattle Republican listed him as an "Unknown Negro, near Savannah, Ga."

Georgia papers followed the manhunt daily, calling Claus "the negro fiend" and expecting a lynching. The Atlanta Constitution headed the first report "Outlook for Lynching Near Darien Junction Promising," and the Brunswick Daily News wrote that he "will hardly be tried by the courts." The Savannah Morning News announced "Claus Lynched Near Eastman," and weekly news digests in several states repeated that he died in his accuser's presence.

Once the wires reported a mistake, the New-York Tribune's subhead read "Impartial Mob May Now Lynch the Right One," the Fredericksburg Free Lance called it "one of the great evils of lynching," and The State, reprinted in the Lancaster Ledger, mocked "the beauties of lynching." Leslie's Weekly, quoted by the Savannah Morning News, wrote that the victim was "a respectable colored man" chased "like a wild beast across seven counties."

The Black papers found took up the story only as the killing of an innocent man. The Wichita Searchlight ran "Innocent Negro Lynched," stressing that he had begged for time to bring alibi witnesses, and the Chicago Broad Ax cited it against ministers who called the South safer for Black people.

The Eastman dispatch and the Savannah Morning News said the dead man was Claus, "positively identified," while the later wires and Leslie's Weekly said he had never seen the woman. Reports also disagree about Claus: the Sun said he was in jail, the Tribune that officers had gone for him, and the Hopkinsville Kentuckian that "the real Ed Claus is still at large." Georgia papers named the woman Minnie Johnson; later wires called her Susie Johnson, a school teacher.

reader.title: Lynching of an unidentified man near Eastman, Georgia
bases: A mob of about fifty men caught a Black man asleep in a swamp near Eastman, hanged him and shot his body, believing him to be Ed Claus, accused of assaulting a white woman (A9, A11, A16).

The Eastman dispatch and later wires report a man hanged and shot to death by a mob of about fifty with no lawful authority, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A9, A11, A16); whether the dead man was Claus is contested, but not the killing (A15, A26).

The Eastman dispatch, the Savannah Morning News, and the July 26 Atlanta and Savannah wires independently report the killing near Eastman (A9, A11, A15, A16); only the Brunswick Daily News doubted it at first (A12), and the dead man's identity is contested.

framing.detail: Georgia papers called Claus 'the negro fiend', headed a report 'Outlook for Lynching Near Darien Junction Promising', and said he 'will hardly be tried by the courts'.
The Savannah Morning News reported the killing as 'Claus Lynched Near Eastman. Paid the Penalty'.
After the wrong-man reports, the Free Lance, Philadelphia Record and Leslie's Weekly condemned the mob; the Tribune headlined 'Impartial Mob May Now Lynch the Right One'.
The State (via Lancaster Ledger) mocked 'the beauties of lynching' while warning that the right man usually goes free to 'prey on other victims'.
Wichita Searchlight headed it 'Innocent Negro Lynched' and called the mob merciless; the Broad Ax used it against ministers who called the South safer.
